source: Two arcs make an eye
videos.handover: Keep the question open: the next topic finds the two centres exactly and names the line through them.
videos.note: The chapter opener: two eyes drawn with arcs and the question of where the arc centres go, left open.

source: XY is a line segment. Using only a ruler and a compass, find

items.question: XY is a line segment. Using only a ruler and a compass, find the centres A and B for the two arcs of an eye with corners X and Y, and draw the eye.
steps: Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY.
With centre X, draw an arc above XY and an arc below XY.
With centre Y and the same radius, draw arcs that cut the first two arcs.
Name the meeting point above XY as A and the one below XY as B. Then AX = AY = BX = BY.
With centre A and radius AX, draw the lower arc from X to Y.
With centre B and the same radius, draw the upper arc from X to Y. The two arcs make the eye.
items.answer: A and B are the meeting points of equal arcs from X and Y; the arc centred at A is the lower arc and the arc centred at B is the upper arc

videos.answer: A and B are the meeting points of equal arcs from X and Y; the arc centred at A is the lower arc and the arc centred at B is the upper arc

source: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at

items.question: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of XY and that AB is perpendicular to XY.
steps: In ΔABX and ΔABY: AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common. So ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by the SSS condition.
Corresponding parts are equal, so ∠XAB = ∠YAB, that is, ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
In ΔAOX and ΔAOY: AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO, and AO is common. So ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by the SAS condition.
Corresponding parts are equal, so OX = OY: O is the midpoint of XY.
Also ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and together they make a straight angle of 180°.
So each of ∠AOX and ∠AOY is half of 180°, which is 90°.
items.answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY

videos.answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY

source: A point P is the same distance from X and Y, that is, PX = P

items.question: A point P is the same distance from X and Y, that is, PX = PY. Justify that P lies on the perpendicular bisector AB of XY.
steps: If P is on the same side of XY as A, pair P with B; otherwise pair P with A. Say we pair P with B.
Then PX = PY and BX = BY, so P and B are each equally far from X and Y.
In ΔPBX and ΔPBY: PX = PY, BX = BY, and PB is common, so ΔPBX ≅ ΔPBY by SSS.
So ∠XPB = ∠YPB, and if PB meets XY at O, then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS (PX = PY, equal angles at P, PO common). So OX = OY and the angles at O are 90°.
So the line PB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
XY has only one perpendicular bisector, the line AB, so P lies on AB.
items.answer: The line through P and B is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS); XY has only one perpendicular bisector, so P lies on AB

videos.answer: The line through P and B is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS); XY has only one perpendicular bisector, so P lies on AB

source: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector

items.question: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and mark the midpoint of XY.
steps: Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY, so that the arcs will meet.
With centre X, draw a long arc above XY. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc above XY that cuts it. Name the meeting point A.
Keep the same radius. With centres X and Y, draw two arcs below XY that cut each other at B.
Join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Mark O where AB crosses XY. O is the midpoint of XY, and ∠AOX = 90°.
Reason: AX = AY and BX = BY, so ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS and then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS.
items.answer: AB, the line through the two meeting points of equal arcs, is the perpendicular bisector; it meets XY at its midpoint O

videos.answer: AB, the line through the two meeting points of equal arcs, is the perpendicular bisector; it meets XY at its midpoint O

source: Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q1

items.question: When constructing the perpendicular bisector, is it necessary to have the same radius for the arcs above and below XY? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer. [Hint 1: Any point that is of the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector. Hint 2: We can draw the whole line if any two of its points are known.]
steps: Construct: arcs of radius r from X and Y above XY meet at A, so AX = AY.
Arcs of a different radius s from X and Y below XY meet at B, so BX = BY.
A is equally far from X and Y, so A lies on the perpendicular bisector. B is equally far from X and Y, so B lies on it too.
Why: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS (AX = AY, BX = BY, AB common), so ∠XAO = ∠YAO; then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS (AX = AY, equal angles at A, AO common), so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°.
Two points fix a whole line, so AB is the perpendicular bisector.
items.answer: No. The radius above may differ from the radius below; A and B are each equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and two points fix the line

videos.answer: No. The radius above may differ from the radius below; A and B are each equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and two points fix the line

source: Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q2

items.question: Is it necessary to construct the pairs of arcs above and below XY? Instead, can we construct both the pairs of arcs on the same side of XY? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
steps: Construct: arcs of radius r from X and Y above XY meet at A.
Arcs of a larger radius s from X and Y, also above XY, meet at a second point P. The radii must differ, or the arcs meet at A again.
AX = AY and PX = PY, so A and P are each equally far from X and Y.
Why: by SSS, ΔAPX ≅ ΔAPY (AX = AY, PX = PY, AP common), so line AP makes equal angles with AX and AY; then SAS on the triangles at the meeting point O gives OX = OY and two 90° angles.
So the line AP, extended to cross XY, is the perpendicular bisector.
items.answer: No. Both pairs can be on the same side if the two radii are different; each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and the line through them, extended, is the perpendicular bisector

videos.answer: No. Both pairs can be on the same side if the two radii are different; each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and the line through them, extended, is the perpendicular bisector

source: Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q3

items.question: While constructing one pair of intersecting arcs, is it necessary that we use the same radii for both of them? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
steps: Construct: an arc of radius r from X and an arc of a different radius s from Y meet at a point P.
Then PX = r and PY = s, so PX ≠ PY.
Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equally far from X and Y: if Q is on it and QO meets XY at O, then ΔQOX ≅ ΔQOY by SAS (OX = OY, ∠QOX = ∠QOY = 90°, QO common), so QX = QY.
P is not equally far from X and Y, so P is not on the perpendicular bisector.
So a line through P is not the perpendicular bisector.
items.answer: Yes. Within one pair the two arcs must have the same radius; otherwise the meeting point is not equally far from X and Y, and every point of the perpendicular bisector is (SAS), so it would not lie on the perpendicular bisector

videos.answer: Yes. Within one pair the two arcs must have the same radius; otherwise the meeting point is not equally far from X and Y, and every point of the perpendicular bisector is (SAS), so it would not lie on the perpendicular bisector

source: Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle

items.question: Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O using only a ruler and a compass, and say why the angle is 90°.
steps: With centre O and any radius, draw arcs that cut the line at X and at Y. Then OX = OY.
Open the compass wider than OX. With centre X, draw an arc above the line.
With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at A. Then AX = AY.
Join O and A. ∠AOX is the required 90° angle.
Reason: in ΔAOX and ΔAOY, AX = AY, OX = OY, and AO is common, so ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS.
So ∠AOX = ∠AOY. Together they make 180°, so each is 90°.
items.answer: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle

videos.answer: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle

source: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a comp

items.question: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the two parts are equal.
steps: With centre O and any radius, draw an arc that cuts OY at A and OX at B. Then OA = OB.
With centre A and a radius long enough for the arcs to meet, draw an arc inside the angle.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at C. Then AC = BC.
Join O and C.
In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
So ∠AOC = ∠BOC, and OC bisects ∠XOY.
items.answer: OC bisects ∠XOY, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS

videos.answer: OC bisects ∠XOY, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS

source: Eight equal petals meet at a centre, along eight equally spa

items.question: Eight equal petals meet at a centre, along eight equally spaced supporting lines. Find the angle between neighbouring lines, and construct it with a ruler and a compass.
steps: The eight angles round the centre are equal and make a full turn of 360°.
The full turn of 360° shared by 8 equal angles gives 45° each.
Draw a line and mark the centre O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O with equal arcs.
Bisect the 90° angle: arcs from O cut the two arms at A and B, then equal arcs from A and B meet at C. OC makes 45° with each arm (SSS).
Extend the two arms and the bisector through O, and bisect one more right angle; this gives four lines, which is eight half-lines from O at 45° to each other.
items.answer: Each angle is 45°; construct 90° and bisect it

videos.answer: Each angle is 45°; construct 90° and bisect it

source: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q1

items.question: Construct at least 4 different angles. Draw their bisectors.
steps: Draw four angles of clearly different sizes, for example a small acute angle, a right angle made with equal arcs, a large acute angle and an obtuse angle.
For each angle with vertex O: with centre O draw an arc that cuts the arms at A and B, so OA = OB.
With one radius, draw arcs from A and from B that meet at C inside the angle.
Join OC. It is the bisector, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
Check: fold the paper along OC; the two arms land on each other.
items.answer: Each bisector is OC, where OA = OB and AC = BC; ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, so the two halves are equal

videos.answer: Each bisector is OC, where OA = OB and AC = BC; ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, so the two halves are equal

source: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q3

items.question: In Step 2 of angle bisection, if arcs of equal radius are drawn on the other side, so that the arcs from A and B meet at a point C on the far side of the vertex O, outside the angle, will the line OC still be an angle bisector? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
steps: Mark A and B on the arms with OA = OB.
With a radius larger than OA, draw equal arcs from A and B on the far side of O; they meet at C, with AC = BC.
In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common.
So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, and ∠AOC = ∠BOC.
Extend CO beyond O to a point D inside ∠AOB. ∠AOD and ∠AOC make a straight angle, and so do ∠BOD and ∠BOC.
So ∠AOD = 180° − ∠AOC and ∠BOD = 180° − ∠BOC; these are equal, so the line CO, extended beyond O, bisects ∠AOB.
items.answer: Yes. OA = OB, AC = BC and OC is common, so ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS and ∠AOC = ∠BOC; their supplements are equal too, so the line CO, extended beyond O, still bisects ∠AOB

videos.answer: Yes. OA = OB, AC = BC and OC is common, so ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS and ∠AOC = ∠BOC; their supplements are equal too, so the line CO, extended beyond O, still bisects ∠AOB

source: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4

items.question: What are the other angles that can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct 65.5° angle?
steps: From 180° by halving: 90°. From 90° by halving: 45°, 22.5°, and so on.
Sums of these also work, for example 90° + 45° = 135° and 45° + 22.5° = 67.5°.
Every angle made this way, doubled enough times, becomes a whole multiple of 45°.
65.5° doubled is 131°, and every further doubling is 131° times a power of 2, which is never a multiple of 45°, because 131 is not divisible by 3 or by 5.
So 65.5° cannot be constructed by bisection.
Later in this chapter we build a 60° angle; halving it gives 30° and 15°, and sums such as 75°. Those all double into multiples of 15°, and 131° times a power of 2 is not one of them either.
items.answer: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made (and, once 60° is built, 30°, 15° and 75°); 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°, or even of 15°

videos.answer: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made (and, once 60° is built, 30°, 15° and 75°); 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°, or even of 15°

source: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q6

items.question: Construct the following figure: a square with four equal petals inside it, each petal running from the centre of the square to one corner. How do we construct the petals so that they are of the maximum possible size within a given square?
steps: Construct a square: a segment, right angles at both ends, equal sides cut with the compass, and join the fourth side.
Find the midpoint of each side by constructing its perpendicular bisector.
The two bisectors through opposite midpoints cross at the centre of the square.
With centre the midpoint of one side and radius half the side, draw a semicircle inside the square. It passes through the two corners at the ends of that side and through the centre.
Do the same from the other three midpoints. Each petal is where two semicircles overlap, from the centre to a corner.
These arcs just touch the sides of the square at the corners, so the petals are as large as they can be.
items.answer: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

videos.answer: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

source: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a p

items.question: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a point X using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the copy is equal.
steps: With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at B and C. Then AB = AC.
Draw a ray from X. With centre X and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at Z. Then XZ = AB.
Open the compass to the length BC.
With centre Z and radius BC, cut the arc at Y. Then YZ = BC and XY = AC.
Join X and Y.
In ΔABC and ΔXYZ: AB = XZ, AC = XY, BC = ZY. So ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, and ∠YXZ = ∠CAB.
items.answer: ∠YXZ is a copy of ∠A, because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS

videos.answer: ∠YXZ is a copy of ∠A, because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS

source: Figure it Out (copying an angle), Q1

items.question: Construct at least 4 different angles in different orientations without taking any measurement. Make a copy of all these angles.
steps: Draw four angles with the ruler only, each in a different direction on the page, for example one opening upwards, one sideways, one downwards and one slanting.
For each angle with vertex A: draw an arc from A cutting the arms at B and C.
Draw a new ray from a point X, and with the same radius draw an arc from X cutting it at Z.
Open the compass to BC, and from Z cut the arc at Y. Join XY.
Each copy is equal because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS. Check by laying tracing paper over both.
items.answer: For each angle, equal arcs from A and X and the chord BC moved to ZY give ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, so every copy equals its angle

videos.answer: For each angle, equal arcs from A and X and the chord BC moved to ZY give ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, so every copy equals its angle

source: A line m and a point B not on it are given. Construct a line

items.question: A line m and a point B not on it are given. Construct a line through B parallel to m using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: Draw a line l through B that cuts m at A. l is the transversal.
With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts m at C and cuts l at D, on the part of l between A and B.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts l at F, on the side of B away from A, as for the matching corner.
Open the compass to CD. With centre F, cut the arc at E, on the same side of l as C.
Draw the line n through B and E. ΔBFE ≅ ΔADC by SSS, so the angle at B equals the angle at A.
These are corresponding angles, so n is parallel to m.
items.answer: The line n through B and E, since the copied corresponding angles are equal (SSS), so n ∥ m

videos.answer: The line n through B and E, since the copied corresponding angles are equal (SSS), so n ∥ m

source: Figure it Out (parallel lines), Q1

items.question: Construct 4 pairs of parallel lines in different orientations.
steps: Draw four lines m in different directions: across, up and down, and two slanting ways.
For each, mark a point B off the line and draw a transversal l through B cutting m at A.
Equal arcs from A and B; the chord CD at A is transferred to the arc at B to give E.
Draw n through B and E. ΔADC ≅ ΔBFE by SSS, so the corresponding angles are equal.
So each n is parallel to its m.
items.answer: Four pairs m and n, each made by copying the corresponding angle at A to B (SSS), so each n ∥ m

videos.answer: Four pairs m and n, each made by copying the corresponding angle at A to B (SSS), so each n ∥ m

source: Six congruent equilateral triangles are placed round a centr

items.question: Six congruent equilateral triangles are placed round a centre O. Do they fit with no gap and no overlap, and is the outer figure a regular hexagon?
steps: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
At O, six such angles meet, and 6 × 60 = 360, the complete angle round a point.
So the six triangles fit round O with no gap and no overlap.
The six outer sides are sides of congruent triangles, so they are all equal.
At each outer corner, two angles of 60° meet, making 120°. So all six angles are equal.
Equal sides and equal angles: the outer figure is a regular hexagon.
items.answer: Yes: six 60° angles make 360°, so they fit; the hexagon has equal sides and every angle is 120°

videos.answer: Yes: six 60° angles make 360°, so they fit; the hexagon has equal sides and every angle is 120°

source: Angles of 40°, 60°, 50°, 30°, 40° and 90° are placed round a

items.question: Angles of 40°, 60°, 50°, 30°, 40° and 90° are placed round a point O, leaving a gap ∠AOI. Find the gap angle. Will a 70° angle fit into the gap?
steps: All the angles round a point add up to 360°.
The six known angles add to 310°.
So the gap angle is 360° − 310° = 50°.
70° is more than 50°, so the 70° angle would overlap its neighbours.
items.answer: The gap is 50°, so the 70° angle does not fit

videos.answer: The gap is 50°, so the 70° angle does not fit

source: In a regular hexagon ABCDEF made of six equilateral triangle

items.question: In a regular hexagon ABCDEF made of six equilateral triangles round the centre O, explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines.
steps: At O, ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠COD are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is 60°.
An angle of 180° is a straight angle, so OA and OD point in opposite directions: AOD is a straight line.
In the same way ∠BOE = 180° and ∠COF = 180°.
So BOE and COF are straight lines too.
items.answer: Each of ∠AOD, ∠BOE and ∠COF is three 60° angles, which is 180°, a straight angle

videos.answer: Each of ∠AOD, ∠BOE and ∠COF is three 60° angles, which is 180°, a straight angle

source: Construct a 60° angle at A on a segment AX using only a rule

items.question: Construct a 60° angle at A on a segment AX using only a ruler and a compass, and explain why it is 60°.
steps: With centre A and any radius, draw a long arc that cuts AX at B.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the first arc at C.
Join A and C. ∠CAX is the required angle.
Join B and C. AB = AC, because both are radii of the first arc.
BA = BC, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
So AB = BC = CA: ΔABC is equilateral, and each of its angles is 60°. So ∠CAX = 60°.
items.answer: ∠CAX = 60°, because ΔABC has three equal sides and so is equilateral

videos.answer: ∠CAX = 60°, because ΔABC has three equal sides and so is equilateral

source: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a

items.question: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: Draw a line and mark A on it. Mark X on the line to the right of A.
With centre A and any radius, draw a large arc that cuts AX at B.
With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60°.
With centre C and the same radius, cut the arc again at D. Then ∠DAC = 60°, by the same equilateral triangle reason.
Join A and D. ∠DAX = 60° + 60° = 120°.
Check: D lies on the side away from X, and the angle between AD and the line on the left is 180° − 120° = 60°.
items.answer: ∠DAX = 120°, made of two 60° angles from equilateral triangles

videos.answer: ∠DAX = 120°, made of two 60° angles from equilateral triangles

source: Construct a regular hexagon with side 4 cm using a ruler and

items.question: Construct a regular hexagon with side 4 cm using a ruler and a compass.
steps: Open the compass to 4 cm using the ruler, and draw a circle with centre O.
Mark a point A on the circle.
With centre A and radius 4 cm, cut the circle at B. ΔOAB is equilateral, so ∠AOB = 60°.
With centre B, cut the circle at C; with centre C, cut at D; then E and F in the same way.
Six angles of 60° at O make 360°, so the sixth step lands back on A.
Join A, B, C, D, E, F in order. Every side is 4 cm and every angle is 60° + 60° = 120°.
items.answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 4 cm and six angles of 120°

videos.answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 4 cm and six angles of 120°

source: Construct a regular hexagon with side 5 cm using the 120° co

items.question: Construct a regular hexagon with side 5 cm using the 120° construction at each corner.
steps: Draw AB = 5 cm with the ruler.
At B, construct 120° between BA and a new ray: two 60° steps with equal arcs. Cut the ray at C with BC = 5 cm.
At C, construct 120° in the same way, turning the same direction, and cut CD = 5 cm.
Repeat at D and E to get E and F with DE = EF = 5 cm.
Join F to A. The angles of a regular hexagon add to 6 × 120 = 720 degrees, and FA comes out 5 cm.
All six sides are 5 cm and all six angles are 120°.
items.answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 5 cm and six angles of 120°

videos.answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 5 cm and six angles of 120°

source: Construct a 30° angle at a point A on a line, using only a r

items.question: Construct a 30° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the line at B.
With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60° (ΔABC is equilateral).
Now bisect ∠CAB: with one radius, draw arcs from B and from C that meet at D inside the angle.
Join A and D.
AB = AC, BD = CD and AD is common, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS.
So ∠DAB = ∠DAC, and each is half of 60°, which is 30°.
items.answer: ∠DAB = 30°: a 60° angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected (SSS)

videos.answer: ∠DAB = 30°: a 60° angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected (SSS)

source: Construct a 15° angle at a point A on a line, using only a r

items.question: Construct a 15° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: Construct ∠CAB = 60° with two equal arcs, and bisect it to get the ray AD with ∠DAB = 30°.
The first arc from A cuts AD at a point E. Then AB = AE.
With one radius, draw arcs from B and from E that meet at F inside ∠DAB.
Join A and F.
AB = AE, BF = EF and AF is common, so ΔABF ≅ ΔAEF by SSS.
So ∠FAB is half of 30°, which is 15°.
items.answer: ∠FAB = 15°: 60° bisected to 30°, then bisected again (SSS each time)

videos.answer: ∠FAB = 15°: 60° bisected to 30°, then bisected again (SSS each time)

source: A six-pointed star has outer points A, B, C, D, E, F and an

items.question: A six-pointed star has outer points A, B, C, D, E, F and an inner regular hexagon GHIJKL. Are the six point triangles ΔAGH, ΔBHI, ΔCIJ, ΔDJK, ΔELK and ΔFLG equilateral? Why?
steps: The inner figure GHIJKL is a regular hexagon, so each of its angles is 120°.
In ΔAGH, side GH is a side of the hexagon, and AG and AH lie along the extended sides LG and IH.
∠AGH and ∠LGH make a straight angle, so ∠AGH = 180° − 120° = 60°.
In the same way ∠AHG = 180° − 120° = 60°.
The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so ∠GAH = 180° − 60° − 60° = 60°.
All three angles are 60°, so ΔAGH is equilateral; the same reasoning works for the other five points.
items.answer: Yes. Each base angle is 180° − 120° = 60°, so all three angles are 60° and each point is an equilateral triangle

videos.answer: Yes. Each base angle is 180° − 120° = 60°, so all three angles are 60° and each point is an equilateral triangle

source: Figure it Out (special angles), Q4

items.question: Draw a line l and mark a point P anywhere outside the line. Construct a perpendicular to the given line l through P. [Hint: Find a line segment on l whose perpendicular bisector passes through P.]
steps: With centre P and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts l at two points X and Y. Then PX = PY.
P is equally far from X and Y, so P lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
With centres X and Y and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of l that meet at Q. Then QX = QY.
Join P and Q; PQ meets l at O.
ΔPXQ ≅ ΔPYQ by SSS, so ∠XPO = ∠YPO; then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS, so ∠POX = ∠POY = 90°.
So PQ is the perpendicular to l through P.
items.answer: Cut l at X and Y with an arc from P, then find Q with QX = QY; PQ is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS), so it is perpendicular to l and passes through P

videos.answer: Cut l at X and Y with an arc from P, then find Q with QX = QY; PQ is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS), so it is perpendicular to l and passes through P

source: Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles? Show one way.

items.question: Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles? Show one way.
steps: The grid has 4 × 6 = 24 unit squares, and each tile covers 2, so 12 tiles are needed.
Each column has 4 squares, one above another.
Two vertical tiles cover one column exactly.
Do this for all 6 columns: 6 × 2 = 12 tiles, with no gap and no overlap.
items.answer: Yes: 12 vertical tiles, 2 in each column

videos.answer: Yes: 12 vertical tiles, 2 in each column

source: Can a 4 × 7 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?

items.question: Can a 4 × 7 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
steps: The grid has 4 × 7 = 28 unit squares, an even number, so 14 tiles would be needed.
Each of the 7 columns has 4 squares.
Two vertical tiles cover each column.
7 columns use 7 × 2 = 14 tiles, with no gap and no overlap.
items.answer: Yes: 14 vertical tiles, 2 in each column

videos.answer: Yes: 14 vertical tiles, 2 in each column

source: Prove that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.

items.question: Prove that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
steps: The grid has 5 × 7 = 35 unit squares.
Each tile covers exactly 2 unit squares, with no overlap.
So any number of tiles covers an even number of squares.
35 is odd, so it is not a number of squares that tiles can cover exactly.
So there is no tiling of the 5 × 7 grid.
items.answer: Not possible: tiles always cover an even number of squares, and 35 is odd

videos.answer: Not possible: tiles always cover an even number of squares, and 35 is odd

items.question: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if both m and n are even? Give a strategy.
steps: Each column has m squares, and m is even.
Cover each column with m ÷ 2 vertical tiles.
Every column is covered, so the whole grid is covered with no gaps or overlaps.
For example, a 6 × 4 grid uses 3 vertical tiles in each of 4 columns, 12 tiles in all.
items.answer: Yes: cover each column with vertical tiles

videos.answer: Yes: cover each column with vertical tiles

source: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if one of m and n

items.question: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if one of m and n is even and the other is odd? Give a strategy.
steps: If the number of rows m is even, cover each column with vertical tiles, as before.
If instead the number of columns n is even, each row has an even number of squares.
Then cover each row with n ÷ 2 horizontal tiles.
For example, a 3 × 4 grid: each of the 3 rows takes 2 horizontal tiles, 6 tiles in all.
items.answer: Yes: use vertical tiles along the even side's columns, or horizontal tiles along rows of even length

videos.answer: Yes: use vertical tiles along the even side's columns, or horizontal tiles along rows of even length

source: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if both m and n a

items.question: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if both m and n are odd? Give reasons.
steps: The number of unit squares is m × n.
An odd number times an odd number is odd, for example 3 × 5 = 15.
Each tile covers 2 squares, so tiles always cover an even number of squares.
An odd number of squares can never be covered exactly.
items.answer: No: m × n is odd, and tiles always cover an even number of squares

videos.answer: No: m × n is odd, and tiles always cover an even number of squares

items.question: A 5 × 3 grid (5 rows, 3 columns) has its top right square removed. Can the remaining 14 squares be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
steps: 14 squares would need 7 tiles.
Top row: the two squares left form one horizontal tile.
Rows 2 and 3: put a vertical tile in each of the 3 columns.
Rows 4 and 5: put a vertical tile in each of the 3 columns.
That is 1 + 3 + 3 = 7 tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.
items.answer: Yes: 1 horizontal tile in the top row and 6 vertical tiles below

videos.answer: Yes: 1 horizontal tile in the top row and 6 vertical tiles below

source: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its second row removed

items.question: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its second row removed. Can the remaining squares be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
steps: 14 squares would need 7 tiles.
Row 1: the left two squares form one horizontal tile.
The top right square goes with the square below it: one vertical tile.
The left square of row 2 goes with the left square of row 3: one vertical tile.
The middle and right squares of row 3 form one horizontal tile.
Rows 4 and 5: one vertical tile in each of the 3 columns.
That is 4 tiles above and 3 tiles below, 7 tiles with no gaps and no overlaps.
items.answer: Yes: a tiling with 7 tiles exists

videos.answer: Yes: a tiling with 7 tiles exists

source: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its top row removed. C

items.question: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its top row removed. Colour it like a chessboard with white corners, and decide whether it can be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
steps: With white corners, the full 5 × 3 grid has 8 white and 7 black squares.
The top middle square sits between two white corners, so it is black.
After removing it, 8 white and 6 black squares are left.
Each 2 × 1 tile covers two neighbouring squares, and neighbours have different colours, so each tile covers one white and one black.
7 tiles would cover 7 white and 7 black squares, but there are 8 white and 6 black.
So no tiling exists.
items.answer: Not tileable: 8 white and 6 black squares remain, but every tile covers one of each

videos.answer: Not tileable: 8 white and 6 black squares remain, but every tile covers one of each

source: Use the colouring to find another unit square that, when rem

items.question: Use the colouring to find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable.
steps: Colour the 5 × 3 grid with white corners: 8 white and 7 black squares.
Removing any black square leaves 8 white and 6 black, which no set of tiles can cover.
The black squares are the ones whose row number plus column number is odd.
Besides the top middle square, these are: row 2, column 1; row 2, column 3; row 3, column 2; row 4, column 1; row 4, column 3; row 5, column 2.
For example, removing the square in row 2, column 1 makes the grid non-tileable.
items.answer: Any black square works, for example row 2, column 1; the others are row 2 column 3, row 3 column 2, row 4 column 1, row 4 column 3 and row 5 column 2

videos.answer: Any black square works, for example row 2, column 1; the others are row 2 column 3, row 3 column 2, row 4 column 1, row 4 column 3 and row 5 column 2

items.question: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: 12 unit squares in 4 rows, where the top two rows have 2 squares each, at the left, and the bottom two rows have 4 squares each. Tile: an L shape of 3 unit squares (two squares stacked, with one more square beside the bottom one). The tile may be turned.
steps: 12 squares need 4 tiles of 3 squares.
One way: cover the top left square with an L that also covers the square beside it and the square below it, in rows 1 and 2.
Then row 2, column 2 is left in the top part; cover it with row 3, columns 2 and 3, in an L.
Row 3, column 1 goes with row 4, columns 1 and 2, in an L.
Row 3, column 4 goes with row 4, columns 3 and 4, in an L.
All 12 squares are covered by 4 tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.
items.answer: Yes, it is possible: four L tiles, turned to different positions

videos.answer: Yes, it is possible: four L tiles, turned to different positions

source: Figure it Out (tiling), Q2

items.question: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: an 8 × 8 grid with the top right corner square and the bottom left corner square removed. Tile: 2 × 1.
steps: The region has 64 squares minus 2, which is 62 squares, an even number.
Colour it like a chessboard. In an 8 × 8 board, the top right and bottom left corners have the same colour, say black.
The full board has 32 white and 32 black squares. Removing two black ones leaves 32 white and 30 black.
Each 2 × 1 tile covers one white and one black square.
31 tiles would cover 31 of each colour, but the counts are 32 and 30.
So the region cannot be tiled.
items.answer: Not possible: the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving 32 of one colour and 30 of the other

videos.answer: Not possible: the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving 32 of one colour and 30 of the other

items.question: Explain why squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons can each tile the whole plane.
steps: Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill the full 360° with no gap and no overlap.
A square has angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares fill a corner.
An equilateral triangle has angles of 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360, so six triangles fill a corner.
A regular hexagon has angles of 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360, so three hexagons fill a corner.
Repeating these corners in every direction covers the whole plane.
items.answer: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°

videos.answer: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°
